newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium hits 14-month high, worries over Russia.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium hits 14-month high, worries over Russia.

text.p: World aluminium prices leapt to the highest levels seen since December 1995 on Tuesday, as an already strong market was massaged by concerns over supplies from Russia, analysts said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium hit $1,701 a tonne, up $11 from Monday, and some $150 above levels prevailing at the start of the year.
Traders said there was a question mark over Russian exports to the West, because of calls to curb foreign ownership of the domestic industry.
"Potentially, it is a worrying situation should that happen," analyst Martin Squires of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co said.
Russia's Interior minister Anatoly Kulikov has said Russia should consider slapping import duties on raw materials and tighten control over tolling deals.
Tolling is where Russia imports alumina from the West, smelts it into refined aluminium, which is then exported onto Western markets.
Since the break-up of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, Western companies, such as Trans-World have become major importers of alumina and part-owners of many aluminium concerns.
Analysts were doubtful, however, whether Russian authorities would take such steps, which have implications for exports and foreign exchange earnings.
"The foreign investment is a critical part of the re-structuring of their internal industry," Squires said.
Russian exports to the West have soared since the annual average of 250,000/300,000 tonnes in the late-1980s.
They have plateaued out at around two million tonnes now - the bulk of which is metal that has been toll-smelted.
Nevertheless, the hint of supplies from such an important source coming under question was enough to fuel rises in a market that is now some 31 percent above last October's lows.
"It helped the market firm up in combination with the general market feeling," Squires said.
Alumiminum prices have been gaining recently on investment fund interest, with speculative money moving into a base metals complex that is advancing on all fronts.

Also, there has been good end-user demand in the U.S., Europe, and the Far East, with appreciable premiums being seen for physical metal which is widely used in transport, packaging and building industries.
"There has been talk of people buying in the expectation that it will move above $1,700. I would not be surprised to see prices at $1,800/1,850 during the next quarter," Squires said.
